title: Concrete Scanning Spokane: GPR Before You Cut
excerpt: Professional concrete scanning in Spokane using ground-penetrating radar. Northwest Concrete Cutting locates rebar, conduit, and post-tension cables before you cut.

sections.text: Before any drill bit touches a slab or any saw blade meets a wall, concrete scanning Spokane professionals use ground-penetrating radar to map everything hidden inside — rebar, post-tension cables, electrical conduit, plumbing lines, and voids. Concrete scanning Spokane is the step that separates controlled, accurate work from costly emergencies. At Northwest Concrete Cutting, we perform GPR scans on virtually every project we touch, and we recommend the same discipline to every contractor, facility manager, and property owner who contacts us. The data a scan delivers in one hour can prevent damage that takes months and tens of thousands of dollars to repair.

Concrete scanning uses ground-penetrating radar (GPR) technology to create a real-time cross-section view of everything embedded inside a concrete slab or wall. A GPR antenna emits high-frequency electromagnetic pulses that travel through the concrete and bounce back when they hit changes in material density — steel reinforcement, plastic conduit, copper pipe, post-tension cables, voids, and areas of moisture intrusion. The return signals are captured and displayed immediately on a screen, giving the technician a continuous subsurface picture as the unit moves across the surface. Unlike concrete X-ray imaging, which involves radioactive isotopes and requires evacuation of surrounding areas, GPR is completely non-destructive, non-hazardous, and safe to perform in occupied buildings and active job sites. Our {{link:/services/concrete-scanning|concrete scanning (GPR) service}} can detect objects embedded up to 18 inches deep in standard-density concrete — deep enough to cover every slab type common to residential, commercial, and industrial construction throughout Eastern Washington and Northern Idaho.
When You Need Scanning Before Cutting or Drilling

The simple rule: any time concrete is being cut, cored, or penetrated, it needs to be scanned first. Whether your project involves {{link:/services/concrete-cutting|concrete cutting services}} for a stairwell opening, coring through a basement slab for new plumbing, sawing control joints in a warehouse floor, or anchoring new equipment to an existing slab, every penetration carries risk when subsurface conditions are unknown. Post-tension cables are the most dangerous unknown in any concrete slab. These high-strength steel strands run through the concrete under enormous tension, and cutting one releases stored energy violently — enough to cause catastrophic structural failure or serious injury to nearby workers. Rebar locations also matter, since diamond blades and core bits can be damaged or destroyed by hitting reinforcement steel at the wrong angle. Electrical conduit, plumbing lines, and data raceways follow paths that may not match original drawings, particularly in structures more than 20 or 30 years old. Concrete scanning Spokane contractors from our team give you a field-verified subsurface map before a single blade touches the slab, eliminating guesswork from the most critical phase of your project.
Why Spokane's Climate Makes Scanning More Critical

Eastern Washington's freeze-thaw cycle is one of the most punishing in the Pacific Northwest. The Spokane region can experience more than 100 freeze-thaw events in a single year, with temperatures swinging repeatedly across the freezing threshold from October through April. That repeated thermal cycling stresses concrete, promotes cracking, and — over decades — causes slabs to shift and settle in ways that displace embedded utilities from their originally designed positions. In older buildings throughout downtown Spokane, the South Hill, Browne's Addition, Peaceful Valley, and the West Central neighborhood, freeze-thaw damage and decades of soil movement mean what's inside a slab may bear little resemblance to any as-built drawing — if those drawings exist at all. Structures built before the 1980s were often constructed without comprehensive utility documentation. In this environment, concrete scanning Spokane professionals treat every slab as an unknown until proven otherwise. Skipping a scan to save a few hundred dollars routinely results in emergency repairs costing $10,000 to $50,000 or more, OSHA recordable incidents, project shutdowns, and liability exposure for the general contractor.

Northwest Concrete Cutting's concrete scanning Spokane workflow is built around efficiency and field-usable results. A certified GPR technician arrives on site with professional-grade scanning equipment calibrated for your slab type, thickness, and aggregate characteristics. The technician walks a systematic grid pattern across the area to be cut or drilled, capturing continuous subsurface data with each pass. Embedded objects — rebar mats, conduit runs, post-tension cable paths, voids — are marked directly on the concrete surface with brightly colored marking paint or chalk immediately as they are detected, giving your cutting crew an on-slab map of what to avoid. You also receive a digital scan report documenting findings, depths, and anomalies, which you can share with your structural engineer, general contractor, or building owner. Residential garage and basement slabs typically scan in under an hour. Commercial floor plates of 5,000 to 10,000 square feet generally take half a day. After the scan, our GPR results feed directly into our {{link:/areas/spokane-wa/concrete-scanning|concrete scanning services in Spokane}}, and we can coordinate seamlessly with our cutting and coring crews to execute the work with full knowledge of what lies below the surface.
GPR Scanning for Commercial and Industrial Projects

Commercial and industrial concrete scanning Spokane projects involve some of the most complex subsurface conditions our technicians encounter. Warehouses, manufacturing facilities, hospitals, school buildings, and multi-story office complexes contain dense networks of utilities embedded in floors and walls — often stacked in multiple layers from multiple build phases over decades. Before {{link:/services/core-drilling|core drilling}} for new mechanical runs, fire suppression risers, or electrical penetrations, a concrete scan identifies every embedded hazard along the planned drill path. We regularly support general contractors and specialty subcontractors across the Spokane metro, including projects in the Spokane Valley industrial corridor, the airport district near Airway Heights, the North Division commercial corridor, and campus expansion projects at universities in Pullman and nearby Moscow, Idaho. Our GPR equipment handles slabs up to 18 inches thick and wall sections up to 12 inches, covering the full range of structural concrete found in Eastern Washington and Northern Idaho commercial construction.
